Received 21 November 2024 l Revised 25 February 2025 l Accepted 4 March 2025 l Published online 11 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between mobile application engagement and lifestyle outcomes, specifically physical activity and dietary habits, during a 36-day virtual competition designed to promote healthier behaviors, including increased physical activity and adherence to a plant-based, whole-food diet. Material and Methods: A secondary data analysis of the ThaiSook prospective cohort study was conducted. Participants were divided into 2 groups based on their engagement with the mobile application: “High-engagement Users” (>50% of challenge days) and “Low-engagement Users” (<50% of challenge days). Results: Among 154 participants (74.7% female; mean age 39.1±10.7 years; median body mass index 23.1 kg/m²), “High-engagement Users” (n=97) had significantly higher average daily step counts (4,921.64±5,721.22 steps) compared to “Low-engagement Users” (n=57) (3,508.81±4,270.00 steps, p-value<0.001). Similarly, High-engagement Users had longer average daily workout durations (35.55±49.59 minutes) than Low-engagement Users (14.14±34.29 minutes, p-value<0.001). High-engagement Users also achieved greater weight loss, with a mean reduction of −0.77 kg. Multiple logistic regression revealed that using the application for more than 18 days was significantly associated with weight loss, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.64 (p-value=0.017). Conclusion: High engagement with a mobile application is positively associated with improved physical activity and weight loss outcomes. These findings underscore the potential of mobile health applications to drive healthier lifestyle behaviors, highlighting the critical role of consistent usage. JSON: Name: mobile_app_engagement_weight_loss Title: Secondary cohort analysis of the association between mobile application engagement and short-term weight change and activity outcomes during a 36-day virtual behavioral challenge Short Hypothesis: Using the mobile application on more than 18 days during the 36-day challenge causes greater mean weight loss and higher average daily step counts than using the mobile application on 18 or fewer days. Related Work: Prior work on mHealth interventions for lifestyle change has shown associations between app-based self-monitoring, gamification, and modest short-term improvements in physical activity and weight. Existing approaches include commercially available behavior-change apps using daily tracking, coach interaction, and monetary or gamified incentives, and clinical apps focused on disease-specific monitoring. Common methodological limitations in prior studies are reliance on self-reported outcomes, brief follow-up windows, nonrandomized designs, heterogeneous engagement metrics, limited objective sensor validation, inadequate control for confounding (including baseline motivation), and selection bias from analyzing only active users. Few studies report dose-response relationships between engagement frequency and outcomes or systematically compare engagement thresholds. Causal inference remains weak in the literature due to lack of randomized assignment and insufficient use of methods such as propensity score adjustment or sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding. Abstract: Problem: Mobile health applications aim to improve physical activity and weight management, but the quantitative relationship between usage frequency and short-term outcomes remains unclear. Approach: We propose a structured secondary analysis of a 36-day virtual challenge dataset collected via the ThaiSook mobile application to evaluate whether app engagement frequency causally relates to weight change and activity. Methods: primary exposure is number of days the app was used; primary outcomes are change in body weight (kg) and average daily steps; covariates include sex, age, baseline BMI, and baseline activity. Contributions: (1) explicit dose-response and threshold analysis of engagement frequency; (2) comparison of logistic, linear mixed, and propensity-score adjusted models; (3) sensitivity analyses for missingness and self-report bias. Expected outcome: quantification of the effect size and statistical significance of a defined engagement threshold (>18 days) on short-term weight loss and activity, clarifying the magnitude and robustness of the engagement–outcome relationship and informing future interventional designs. Experiments: Dataset: ThaiSook 36-day virtual challenge dataset, N≈154 participants with demographics, self-reported baseline BMI, daily logs of app usage days, daily weight entries, daily steps, workout minutes, fruit/veg servings, water intake, and sleep hours. Inclusion: age ≥20, consent, ≥1 baseline and ≥1 end-of-challenge weight entry. Preprocessing: compute exposure variable days_used (0–36), binary high_engagement = days_used>18, compute weight_change = end_weight - baseline_weight, compute mean_daily_steps and mean_daily_exercise_minutes. Handle missingness with two pipelines: complete-case and multiple imputation (MICE, 20 imputations). Baselines for comparison: low_engagement (≤18 days), continuous dose model (per additional day used), and propensity-score matched cohort (1:1 nearest neighbor, caliper 0.2 SD on covariates). Models: (1) linear regression of weight_change on high_engagement adjusted for sex, age group, baseline BMI, baseline steps; (2) logistic regression for any_weight_loss (>0 kg) with same covariates; (3) linear mixed-effects model with daily steps as dependent variable, random intercept per participant, fixed effects for days_used and time; (4) dose-response spline (restricted cubic spline) of days_used vs weight_change. Evaluation metrics: mean difference in kg (95% CI), adjusted odds ratio (95% CI) for any_weight_loss, Cohen's d, R-squared, AIC, and root mean square error for continuous models; average treatment effect from propensity-score matching with bootstrap CIs. Ablation and sensitivity studies: (A) threshold sensitivity grid search (cutpoints 8, 12, 18, 24 days) to report effect heterogeneity; (B) model comparison with and without imputed data; (C) exclude participants with self-reported weight only vs participants with device-logged weight (if available); (D) subgroup analyses stratified by baseline BMI category, sex, and age deciles; (E) E-value calculation and Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding. Significance: two-sided tests, alpha=0.05, adjust for multiple comparisons with Benjamini-Hochberg where applicable. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-report bias: primary outcomes and many predictors are self-reported, producing measurement error and potential differential misclassification. Confounding and reverse causation: motivated participants may both engage more and lose weight, limiting causal inference in absence of randomization; residual unmeasured confounders may bias effect estimates. Selection bias: complete-case analysis may exclude irregular users and dropouts, overestimating effect sizes. Small sample size and demographic imbalance (female majority) limit statistical power for subgroup analyses and external generalizability. Short follow-up (36 days) limits conclusions about sustained weight change and long-term behavior maintenance. Engagement metric granularity: binary thresholding reduces continuous usage information; days_used may not capture quality of engagement (passive vs active logging). Sensor validity and heterogeneity: step counts may be from different devices with variable accuracy. Statistical model limitations: linearity and logistic model assumptions and potential multicollinearity among covariates. Privacy and data completeness constraints may restrict access to device-verified measures for validation.
